title: Separation of Powers and Checks and Balances

blocks.text: Imagine one office that writes the traffic law, arrests you for breaking it and then decides your case. You would have no defence at all. The whole architecture of modern government exists to make sure those three jobs never sit in the same hand.

blocks.markdown:
Government performs three distinct functions, and each is entrusted to a separate organ.

- The **legislature** makes the law.
- The **executive** implements and enforces the law.
- The **judiciary** interprets the law and settles disputes about it.

In Nigeria these powers are formally vested by the 1999 Constitution: legislative power in the National Assembly, executive power in the President, and judicial power in the courts under section 6.

blocks.title: Separation of powers
blocks.text: The doctrine that the legislative, executive and judicial powers of government should be exercised by three separate and independent organs, so that no single body accumulates enough power to become tyrannical. It was systematically stated by the French writer Baron de Montesquieu in The Spirit of the Laws, published in 1748, building on the earlier work of John Locke.

items: The same person should not be a member of more than one organ of government.
One organ should not control or interfere in the work of another organ.
One organ should not perform the functions of another organ.

blocks.markdown:
### Checks and balances

Complete separation would produce three organs unable to restrain one another at all. **Checks and balances** therefore give each organ limited power over the others, so that separation does not become isolation. The result is a system in which every organ is watched by the others.

headers: Checks it exercises on the others (Nigerian examples)
rows: Screens and confirms ministerial, ambassadorial and INEC appointments; passes the Appropriation Act, without which the executive cannot spend; summons officials and conducts oversight investigations; ratifies treaties; can impeach the President for gross misconduct; can override a presidential veto by a two-thirds majority of each chamber
Confirms the appointment of the Chief Justice and Justices of the Supreme Court; can alter the jurisdiction of courts by legislation; approves the judiciary's budget
The President assents to bills or withholds assent; may summon or address the National Assembly; prepares and lays the budget estimates

The President appoints judges on the recommendation of the National Judicial Council and subject to Senate confirmation for the highest courts; exercises the prerogative of mercy to pardon or commute sentences
Through judicial review, declares any Act inconsistent with the Constitution null and void
Declares executive acts ultra vires or unconstitutional; enforces fundamental rights against government; the Chief Justice appoints the panel that investigates an impeachment allegation
blocks.caption: Checks and balances in Nigeria's presidential system

blocks.markdown:
### Merits and limitations

**Merits**: it prevents the concentration of power and so guards against dictatorship; it protects individual liberty and the rule of law; it promotes efficiency, because each organ specialises; and it makes officials accountable, since each is watched by others.

**Limitations**: absolute separation is impossible in practice. **Delegated legislation** lets the executive make rules and regulations, which is a legislative act. The legislature acts judicially when it tries an impeachment or punishes contempt of the House. The judiciary makes law in practice through binding precedent. Party discipline can neutralise legislative oversight where the same party dominates both organs. And separation can produce **deadlock**, as when a budget stalls because the President and the National Assembly cannot agree.

blocks.title: Evaluating whether a constitutional provision respects separation of powers
blocks.prompt: A proposed amendment would allow the President to remove a Justice of the Supreme Court at will, without reference to the National Judicial Council or the Senate. Evaluate this proposal against the doctrine of separation of powers.

steps.text: State the relevant limb of the doctrine. One organ should not control or interfere in the work of another.
Identify what the provision does. It places the tenure of a judicial officer entirely in executive hands, so a judge's continued employment would depend on pleasing the President.

Trace the consequence for judicial independence. A judge who can be dismissed at will cannot safely declare an executive act unconstitutional, so judicial review — the judiciary's principal check on the executive — would collapse.

Compare with the existing safeguard. Under the 1999 Constitution security of tenure, National Judicial Council involvement and retirement at a fixed age of 70 for Supreme Court Justices insulate judges from precisely this pressure.
Give a reasoned conclusion. The proposal violates the doctrine: it converts a check into executive control, and it removes the independence on which the whole system of checks and balances depends.

blocks.answer: The proposal violates separation of powers because it subordinates the judiciary to the executive and destroys the security of tenure that makes judicial review possible

blocks.title: Do not confuse the two ideas
blocks.text: Separation of powers keeps the organs apart; checks and balances let them restrain one another. A common error is to describe impeachment as an example of separation of powers. It is a check — the legislature acting on the executive — and it works precisely because the two organs are separate.

points: Government has three functions — making, executing and interpreting the law — assigned to legislature, executive and judiciary.
The doctrine of separation of powers was systematically stated by Montesquieu in The Spirit of the Laws in 1748.
Its three limbs forbid overlapping membership, interference between organs and the performance of one organ's functions by another.
Checks and balances give each organ limited restraining power over the others, such as legislative confirmation, presidential assent and judicial review.
The doctrine protects liberty and prevents tyranny but cannot be applied absolutely, and it can produce deadlock.
